rv.q: The evening is an absolute banger.
Inter Alia’s impact builds and builds until it’s almost unbearable.
By the final blackout, the verdict is clear: this is a damningly topical and vital drama that needs to be heard.
What is never in doubt is the immense importance of what Miller is tackling or the power of Pike’s performance, which is simply superb.
Pike's Jessica is a force of nature, going out on karaoke nights with girlfriend barristers.
Once again, the piece calls for a transfixing, shape-shifting performance from its star, and the hurtling 105-minute action showcases Pike’s theatrical bravura.
Yet Miller’s play does not live up to the threat of its subject: a teenage boy accused, a family in disarray.
But for all the quality of the production, I have the nagging feeling that deep down it’s really a lecture.
Rosamund Pike sparkles as a beleaguered judge in a clod-hopping feminism-lite drama
Under Justin Martin’s stellar direction, Inter Alia is a play for our time, with no easy answers.
This is a show that continues a vital conversation, and does so with empathy, care and burning conviction.
Masterfully directed by Justin Martin (who also helmed Prima Facie), Pike also relishes a script which beautifully captures the singularity of motherhood.
Pike commands the stage throughout, deftly bringing the audience into her most intimate thoughts and feelings.
It makes a considerable impact, and its actors are excellent, especially Rosamund Pike’s performance, whether commandingly wielding her microphone or playing the paranoid mother.
The whole play offers an energizing, even dazzling, tour de force by its star actor, who’s always charismatic.
Rosamund Pike is a convincing tour de force, giving her central character a wide range of palpable emotions.
The play develops into a gripping whodunnit and the evidence is neatly orchestrated to keep the truth hidden from view.
Rosamund Pike, of 'Saltburn' fame, is vibrantly engaging as the embattled heroine, and her commanding stage presence carries an otherwise pedestrian production.
If this is a politically driven exercise in box-ticking then it's still a thoughtful, provocative, and often amusing project.

This criticism doesn't take away from Pike's energetic and convincing performance, the sterling service provided by Glover and Talbot, or Martin's epic ability to speed things along while keeping us aboard.
The end, however, redeemed it for me.

cn.t: Pike dazzles in Miller's follow-up to Prima Facie, tackling sexual assault and motherhood through a judge's crisis. Critics praise the searing performances and timely themes, though some find it overly didactic and reliant on direct address.
